text:
The review covers three winter seasons of field data from the brake controller fitted to 214 chairlifts across eleven resorts in the Varrow range. The controller, designated BC-7, monitors hydraulic pressure on the disc brake and engages a secondary clamp when it detects a rollback above a set threshold. The panel was asked to explain a cluster of unplanned stops recorded during the 2025 and 2026 seasons and to judge whether the controller's own diagnostics could warn operators before a stop occurs.

The work began after Brennock Mechanical, a maintenance contractor, reported that three lifts had stalled on loaded return runs within a single week. The Alder Valley reliability group was formed that spring and asked Dana Osei to lead the data work. Two lift engineers from the regional safety office joined the panel, which met monthly by video and kept its minutes in a shared archive maintained by the operator's IT staff. The logging agent sampled pressure at 50 hertz and wrote compressed files each night, which made the early months harder to reconcile because two resorts used different clock settings for several weeks. None of this logistics detail changes the findings, but it explains why the first analysis was delayed by about six weeks.

The brake controller itself was designed about eight years earlier by an engineering firm that has since been absorbed into a larger group. The original design documents are incomplete, so the panel relied on the firmware changelog and on informal conversations with two retired technicians to understand how the clamp handover was meant to work. The secondary clamp is a spring-loaded shoe that closes on the brake rotor when hydraulic pressure falls below a set level. Engineers described the handover between the primary disc brake and the clamp as the most delicate part of the sequence, because the two systems must not both act at once.

Unplanned stops were sorted into three groups by the operator's dispatch system: rollbacks above the threshold, emergency stops triggered by a passenger, and stops caused by drive faults. Only the first group was used for the detection analysis. The dispatch codes were entered by hand and were not checked against the controller logs, so a small number of miscoded events may have shifted the counts in either direction. The dispatch system also merges duplicate entries when a lift is restarted within five minutes, which the panel accepted without testing.

The first principal finding concerns early warning. Across 1,862 logged rollback stops, a pressure decay of more than 12 percent in the 4 seconds before a stop appeared in 1,731 cases, a detection rate of 93 percent. The same signature was reproduced separately in each of the three seasons and at each of the eleven resorts, so it does not depend on one site or one cold snap. A holdout set of 240 events from the 2026 season gave a detection rate of 92 percent, close to the main figure. Because the decay appears before the rollback itself, it gives operators a usable window to halt the lift.

The panel's scope was limited in an important way. Every lift in the sample was a detachable quad chairlift, and no fixed-grip or surface lifts were instrumented, so the signature may not transfer to lifts with different brake architectures. The panel also reviewed only controllers running firmware from the 4.x line, which means older hardware was outside the study entirely.

The detection figure carries real uncertainty. The 95 percent confidence interval for the detection rate runs from 91.8 to 94.0 percent under the sampling method used, but that interval assumes that logged stops are a fair sample of all stops. Operators do not log every short stop, so the true rate among all events may be lower. The panel could not estimate how many minor stops went unrecorded.

The panel assumed that the pressure sensors stay within calibration tolerance at temperatures below minus 15 degrees Celsius. That assumption was not tested. The sensors were checked against reference gauges only at the spring service, and no cold chamber trial was run, so the detection figure may be optimistic on the coldest mornings of the season.

One resort disagreed. Logs from the Tarn Hollow site showed no decay signature in February for 38 stops, and the panel could not find a cause in the wiring, the firmware build, or the sensor batch. Engineers suspected a mounting fault on a single bracket but did not confirm it. The panel kept these 38 events in the count as misses and reported the figure both ways in the appendix to the full report, which should be read alongside this summary.

The second principal finding concerns the firmware. Units running revision 4.2 or later recorded a stop-failure rate of 0.4 percent, compared with 6.8 percent on earlier revisions. Here a stop failure means the secondary clamp did not engage within two seconds of the primary brake releasing. The revision changed how the controller samples pressure during the clamp handover, and it removed a timing fault that delayed the clamp by up to 0.8 seconds. This result was reproduced across the same resorts and across both winter seasons, and it held after adjusting for lift age and loading.

Before any operator acts on these results, several conditions should be met. Each unit should be verified in the field against a reference gauge, the pressure threshold should be re-set after a cold trial, and the early-warning signal should be used only as an alert, not as the sole basis for shutting a lift down. The panel recommends that revision 4.2 be installed everywhere before the next season, but that the early-warning alert be validated on each lift type before it is relied on.

The panel will publish the cold chamber protocol in the spring and will extend the sample to fixed-grip lifts if the operator agrees. Those results will be reported separately, and this summary should not be read as covering them. Field teams have been asked to keep the logging agent running during the spring maintenance window so that the next set of data is continuous.

The Harbor Lane Library Systems team evaluated a prototype book recommendation model between March and July of this year. The model was built to suggest titles to patrons who had borrowed at least three books in the previous twelve months across four branch libraries in the fictional Eastmere County consortium. The evaluation was led by a data scientist named Rowan Aldous, supported by two catalogue specialists named Imke Varga and Teodor Lind, and reviewed by a small steering group that met every two weeks. The team wanted to know whether the model could surface titles that patrons would actually borrow, rather than only titles that were already popular with everyone.

The consortium had run a simple popularity list on its homepage since 2019, and that list remained the comparison point throughout the trial. The prototype combined borrowing histories with subject tags drawn from the catalogue, and it used a nearest-neighbour approach to find readers with similar habits. Installation took about six weeks, and most of that time went into cleaning subject headings that different staff members had entered over many years. The team recorded each change in a shared spreadsheet and kept a running list of known problems, which grew to about forty entries by the end of the trial. Some of those entries were minor, such as duplicated spellings of the same genre, while others affected whole collections.

The trial covered 2,113 patrons who were randomly assigned either to see the prototype suggestions or the existing popularity list on their account page. Over the eight-week window, 1,488 patrons had at least one page view of the suggestion panel, and the remaining patrons never scrolled far enough to see it. The primary outcome was whether a patron placed a hold or checked out a suggested title within fourteen days. Early results suggest that patrons who saw the prototype suggestions placed holds or checkouts on a suggested title at a higher rate than those who saw the popularity list, with an observed rate of about 6.4 percent against 4.3 percent. The difference of about 2.1 percentage points has a wide interval, and the lower end of that interval falls slightly below zero.

The sample was small and short for a recommendation system, and the team cannot rule out that the difference reflects the particular eight weeks of the trial. A holiday closure in the second week removed several branches from the schedule, and a new bestseller list was published during the final week. Either event could have shifted borrowing in ways that favoured one arm over the other. The steering group discussed extending the trial but decided that the consortium's budget year would not allow it.

A second observation may matter more for the library than the headline rate. Suggestions from the prototype were more often in subjects that a patron had not borrowed before, with about 31 percent of suggested titles falling outside a patron's earlier subjects, compared with about 12 percent for the popularity list. Patrons who received these unfamiliar suggestions were slightly more likely to borrow a title in a subject they had not tried, although the number of such cases was only 97 and the comparison was not planned in advance.

The model assumed that subject tags meant the same thing at every branch, and that assumption was never tested. The children's collection at one branch had been catalogued by a volunteer using a different scheme for several years, and nobody has yet checked whether that branch received systematically weaker suggestions. Until that check is done, the team cannot say whether the results generalise to every patron group.

Hand review was carried out on a random sample of 200 suggestion lists. The catalogue specialists rated 78 percent of lists as plausible for the patron who received them. Most lists were rated by one reviewer only, so the team has no measure of how much two reviewers would agree. A rough allowance of ten points in either direction seems sensible for that figure, but the number is a judgement rather than a calculation.

The steering group met every two weeks and kept minutes that ran to about thirty pages by July. Its members included the head of collections, a branch manager from the eastern site, and a representative from the volunteer programme, who asked to be included after the children's collection issue came up in April. Decisions were usually made by consensus, although the head of collections had the final word on anything that touched staff workload. The minutes are stored in the consortium's internal document system and are not part of this report.

Logistics took up a surprising share of the project. The prototype ran on a shared virtual machine in the consortium data centre, and nightly retraining took roughly forty minutes. The team kept a rollback script that restored the popularity list within a few minutes if the panel misbehaved, and it was used once, after a cache problem hid the panel for a morning. The consortium's legal office reviewed the licence for the nearest-neighbour library, and the procurement paperwork ran alongside the trial without affecting its schedule.

The analysis also assumes that patrons in the popularity arm did not encounter the prototype panel through other channels. The monthly printed newsletter carried a short list of recommended titles that was drawn from the same data, and the team did not check whether readers had seen it. If they had, the gap between the two arms would be understated, and the true difference could be larger or smaller than reported.

Before any wider rollout, the team recommends three conditions. First, a second trial should run for at least one full academic term. Second, subject tags should be audited at every branch, with the children's collection checked first. Third, an independent reviewer should rate a fresh sample of suggestion lists. Until these conditions are met, the results should be read as a reason to keep testing rather than a reason to change the homepage or the account page. The team also suggested a simple dashboard that shows weekly hold rates for each branch, so that problems in one location cannot hide inside an overall average.

The report does not claim that the prototype is better in general. Its findings describe one consortium, one season, and one outcome measure. A later reader who wants to act on the early signal should first confirm that the conditions above have been met, and should expect the eventual estimate to differ from the one reported here.

The Harrow Bend Water Reclamation District operates three treatment plants serving about 210,000 residents. This review examines dosing deviations recorded between March 2025 and August 2026 at the coagulant feed systems, which use diaphragm metering pumps to inject polyaluminium chloride upstream of the rapid mix basins. The operations committee commissioned the review after the Eastfield plant logged four underdose events in a single quarter, each of which triggered a manual jar test and an assessment for a boil-water advisory that was ultimately not issued.

The maintenance group, led by Ruth Okonkwo-Hale as operations engineering lead, tracked pump faults until early 2025 through a shared spreadsheet kept by two night-shift technicians. The spreadsheet was then replaced by a ticketing tool configured by the vendor integration team, and records from before the migration were partly rebuilt from paper logs. Those rebuilt entries make up roughly 18 percent of the records used in the analysis. The pumps are manufactured by Calder Fluidics, and the district stocks a single diaphragm part number across all three plants, which simplified spares logistics but does not bear on the findings.

The district's jar test procedure is performed by bench technicians at each plant and takes about forty minutes. During the review period it was run on 37 occasions for reasons unrelated to pump faults, mostly routine verification, so the team separated those from the deviation events before counting. Several of the jar tests used water samples collected after the rapid mix basin, which can differ from injection conditions, and the team noted this as a source of noise rather than correcting for it.

Operators on the night shift were interviewed in May 2026 as part of the review. Several described the weekly round as the most reliable point at which to notice drift, since the stroke counter is read by hand and written down before the shift handover. Others said the log was sometimes completed at the end of a long shift, and the team could not measure how often entries were backdated. The interview notes are held by the district records office and were used only for context, not as data.

The investigation compared two maintenance approaches. Under the standard schedule, diaphragms were replaced at a fixed interval of 2,000 operating hours. Under the trial protocol, technicians recorded stroke-count drift and check-valve pressure decay during each weekly round and replaced the diaphragm when either measure crossed a threshold set by the engineering group. Assignment was not randomised at the level of individual pumps. Instead, each plant alternated between the two arms by calendar quarter, which limits but does not remove the chance that seasonal conditions differed between arms.

Each pump-month was counted as one unit regardless of how many hours the pump actually ran, which slightly favours the standard schedule at plants where pumps ran at reduced duty during a quarter. Deviations were defined as any reading more than 5 percent below setpoint for ten consecutive minutes, drawn from the plant historian rather than from operator logs. The review also looked at how alarms were acknowledged. Operators acknowledged most flow alarms within ten minutes, but acknowledgement did not reliably mean that the pump had been inspected, and the review found several cases where an alarm was cleared after a restart without a stroke-count check. These cases were counted as deviations because the setpoint was still missed during the affected interval.

The principal finding is that the condition-triggered protocol reduced dosing deviations at Eastfield and Northmere. Across 1,184 pump-months of operation, the condition-triggered protocol was associated with a reduction in dosing deviations from 0.31 to 0.09 events per pump-month. The 95 percent interval for the difference runs from 0.14 to 0.27 events per pump-month. The direction of the effect was the same in each of the four quarters analysed at those two plants, which the team regards as the main reason to treat the result as established rather than incidental.

A second observation, which the team regards as the more useful for operators, is that deviations clustered in the 72 hours before a diaphragm failure. Stroke volume fell gradually during that window without tripping the flow alarm, because the alarm is set at a 15 percent deviation band. The drift had usually been visible in the weekly stroke-count log two to three weeks earlier, which is why the trial protocol could intervene before failure.

The rebuilt paper records are less complete than the electronic ones. If omitted entries were disproportionately failures, the standard-schedule deviation rate may be understated by an amount the team estimates at between 4 and 11 percent, though they could not verify this.

The study period included a mild winter with lower raw water turbidity, so coagulant demand was also lower, and deviation counts may reflect load as well as pump condition. The team's sensitivity analysis suggested the effect persisted after adjusting for turbidity, but the adjusted interval was wide.

The scope is limited to polyaluminium chloride feed at three plants using one pump model family, and these results should not be assumed to transfer to sodium hypochlorite or fluoride feeds. Those chemicals have different wear and failure patterns.

The team assumed that stroke-count drift is a valid proxy for diaphragm fatigue. Only 11 pumps were torn down to check this, and agreement with inspection findings was moderate, so the mechanism rests on an assumption that was tested only lightly.

Saltmarsh showed no significant difference between the two arms in its first two quarters, and the team attributes this to a chemistry change in the second quarter without confirming that explanation. Saltmarsh's result therefore counts against the finding as much as it supports it, and the committee should not treat the three-plant pattern as uniform. The review was drafted by the process engineering team and reviewed by the district's independent water quality advisor, who asked for the Saltmarsh analysis to be presented separately. The advisor's comments are appended to the committee pack and are not repeated here.

Before any district-wide adoption, the committee should require validation of the check-valve pressure threshold on at least one additional model family and a calibrated flow meter at the injection point, since the current reading depends on the pump's own stroke counter. Until both conditions are met, the protocol should remain a plant-level trial.

This evaluation report describes an early test of a speech-to-text model intended to produce draft notes from recorded calls handled at the Tallowmere contact site. The work was carried out by the Quillfeather evaluation group, a small team of four people who divide their time between data labelling and pipeline maintenance. The model was trained on a general corpus of conversational audio and then adapted with a few hundred hours of internal call recordings. The adaptation settings are held in a separate configuration log, and this report does not reproduce them, because the log was written by the previous group and its notes are only partly complete.

Background on the project is relevant only to explain how the test was run. The speech pipeline was first built about eighteen months earlier by a group that has since moved to other work, and its documentation is partial. The team lead, who holds the decision on what counts as an acceptable result, meets with the operations group every second Thursday, and the test results were presented at one of those meetings. Room bookings for the annotation sessions were arranged through the site office, and the annotators were paid through the standard research contract for the quarter. None of these details affect the numbers reported below, but they explain why some steps were slower than planned.

The test set contained 212 calls drawn from three weeks of recordings in the spring quarter. Calls were selected by a stratified sample across four queue types, namely billing, repairs, cancellations and general enquiries. Each call was transcribed by the model and compared against a reference transcript prepared by a trained annotator. Annotators were given the audio at normal speed only, and replay was limited to two passes per segment. The annotators worked from a shared style guide that was revised twice during the test period, so the reference transcripts were not produced under identical conditions across the full set. Storage for the audio was reorganised in August, and a number of files had to be re-linked by hand before scoring could begin, which took most of one week.

The headline measure was word error rate computed on normalised text, with numerals, dates and product codes scored as separate categories. Across the 212 calls the mean word error rate was 14.8 percent, with a standard deviation of 6.1 points. Performance varied by queue. Billing calls, which tend to contain long strings of digits and spelled-out names, averaged 19.2 percent, while cancellation calls averaged 11.0 percent. These figures are descriptive. The confidence interval on the overall mean is roughly 13.9 to 15.7 percent under a simple bootstrap, but that calculation treats each call as independent and does not account for clustering by agent. The queue-level comparisons should therefore be read as hypotheses to check rather than settled differences.

The clearest pattern in the data concerns structured content. Numerals and product codes accounted for a disproportionate share of errors, with roughly a third of all substitutions falling in those categories despite making up under a tenth of reference tokens. This gap appeared in all four queue types, although its size differed. The reviewers who looked at a sample of the errors noted that many of the failed numerals were close phonetic neighbours of the correct value, such as a run of digits where two adjacent groups were swapped, which suggests the model may be recovering the sound but not the structure of a spoken number.

Calls came from nineteen agents, and a handful of agents accounted for a large share of the test set. One agent, who speaks with a strong regional accent, had an average error rate of 22 percent. Because that agent handled only 31 calls in the sample, the estimate is noisy and could move considerably with a different selection. Speaker-level metadata was not shared with the wider group, so this breakdown was produced and checked only by the evaluation team. Nothing in this report should be taken as a judgement about any individual agent's performance.

Draft notes were also produced by a downstream summariser, which turns the transcript into a short structured record. Two reviewers read a random subset of 140 draft notes and marked each one as acceptable or not acceptable for use in a customer record. Reviewers judged the draft notes acceptable in 71 percent of cases, which suggests that moderate transcription errors are often tolerable for note-taking purposes. The reviewers' agreement was modest, with a kappa of 0.48, and they disagreed most often on notes where a single wrong word changed the meaning of a request. The acceptability figure should be treated as an approximate guide.

The analysis assumes that the reference transcripts are close enough to ground truth to be used as a yardstick. This assumption was not tested with a second independent annotation pass, and it may be optimistic for the billing queue, where annotators reported that digit strings were sometimes hard to hear even on the original recording. If the references contain their own errors, the reported word error rate would be inflated for some categories and understated for others, and the direction of that bias is not known.

The results apply only to recordings made on the current headset setup at the Tallowmere site. Calls routed through other telephony paths use different compression, and nothing in this test establishes how the model would perform on them. The adaptation data also came from a single calendar period, so seasonal changes in call topics may affect performance in ways the test cannot detect.

Before any deployment decision, the evaluation group recommends a larger test of at least 1,000 calls across two sites, with a second annotation pass on a subset to estimate reference noise. The error rate on numerals should also be brought below a threshold agreed with the operations lead, and that threshold has not yet been set. Until these conditions are met, the model should be used only as a drafting aid whose output is read by a person before it enters any record.

Overall, the early results suggest that the model may be useful for draft notes on conversational content, while its handling of numbers remains a weak point. The evidence is tentative. It rests on one small sample, one site, and reviewers who agreed only moderately with each other. Further work should focus on the numeral problem first, since it is the most consistent pattern in the data and the one most likely to matter to the people reading the notes later. The team expects to repeat the test once the larger sample is available, though the date has not been fixed.

The field trial was run by the Lowmoor Soil Systems Group, a small agronomy team based at the Tarn Hollow research station in Orrin County. A regional growers cooperative asked the team to test whether low-cost capacitance probes could replace manual gravimetric sampling when scheduling drip irrigation on sandy loam and clay loam fields. Day-to-day logistics were handled by two field technicians, Dara Osei and Pell Varga, who rotated between sites every nine days. The work was supervised by a principal agronomist, Imre Halloran, who reviewed all calibration data before it was used.

Across two seasons the team installed 214 probes at 31 fields. Each probe was calibrated on site by fitting a local regression against oven-dried soil samples taken at four depths: 10, 20, 40 and 60 centimetres. Calibration sets were collected during the first three weeks of each season and then held fixed for the rest of that season. Sensor readings were logged every fifteen minutes to a regional server operated by the cooperative. The logging scripts were kept in a shared repository maintained by the cooperative's data engineer, Mireille Anand.

In season one, calibrated probe estimates matched gravimetric measurements with a root mean square error of 2.1 percentage points by volume across 9,870 paired observations. The second season was conducted at 17 different fields with a fresh probe lot, and it produced a root mean square error of 2.3 percentage points across 6,412 paired observations. Agreement held across both soil textures and all four depths in each season. The accuracy result was therefore reproduced in an independent set of fields and sensors, and we regard it as clearly established.

The second principal finding concerns water use. Fields that scheduled irrigation from probe readings applied on average 14 percent less water than matched control fields managed on a weekly calendar schedule. Yield differences were not significant in either season. The water saving appeared in both seasons, with similar size, so it is replicated rather than a single-year effect.

Logistics were not always smooth. In season one, 11 of the 214 probes failed, mostly because cable connectors corroded at a single depot where equipment was stored near a wash bay. Failed units were removed from analysis and replaced, and their pre-failure data were retained where they passed the quality checks. The depot was moved in the second season, and no failures were recorded there afterward. Two technicians also reported that the mounting tubes were difficult to seat in stony ground, which slowed installation by roughly a day per field.

The calibration dependence is the main practical limit. Local regressions had to be redone whenever soil texture changed within a field, and the team found that probes installed above a gravel layer below 40 centimetres drifted over the season. The team did not attempt to correct for it, and those probes were excluded from the water-use comparison. A grower applying these results would need to map texture before installation rather than assume one calibration covers a whole field.

Growers in the cooperative were given a short training session on reading the dashboard, which was built by an outside software contractor the cooperative had used before. The dashboard displayed daily moisture estimates and a simple irrigation trigger. Participants reported that it was easiest to use on phones in the field, though several asked for a clearer warning when the battery on a probe was low. Participants were also asked to record every irrigation event in a paper logbook as a cross-check, and the logbooks were transcribed into the study database by Halloran's assistant over the winter.

The yield comparison is less certain than the accuracy result. The 95 percent confidence interval for the yield difference ran from minus 6 percent to plus 3 percent, so the study cannot rule out a modest yield penalty of up to six percent in some crops. Fewer than half of the fields grew the same crop in both seasons, which further widens the uncertainty for crop-specific claims.

The analysis rests on an assumption that was never tested directly. The team assumed that soil salinity stayed below 2 dS/m across the trial fields, because the probe calibration model was not designed for saline conditions. Salinity was measured only once per field at installation and was not tracked afterward. If salinity rose during a season, probe readings could shift in ways that the calibration would not reveal.

Not all prior evidence agrees with these results. A small pilot run the previous year in the neighbouring Kell valley reported larger errors, around 5 percentage points, which it attributed to a different probe lot. The team noted this but could not reproduce it, since the pilot's raw data were not available and its sensors had been discarded. Until that gap is resolved, the pilot should be treated as a warning rather than a refutation.

All trial fields lay in a temperate climate with annual rainfall above 600 millimetres, and most were rain-fed with supplemental irrigation. Results should not be assumed for arid irrigation districts, where salinity, crust formation and deeper root zones may behave differently. The climate gradient within the region was modest, so the study could not test how performance changes across larger distances between fields. Three of the 31 fields were in hilly terrain, and the team lacked enough of them to draw conclusions about slopes.

Before adopting probe-based scheduling, a grower should confirm that soil texture is uniform across the field or mapped in zones, recalibrate at the start of each season, and check salinity with a separate test. The team recommends that these steps be completed before any water-use saving is expected. The findings support the accuracy of calibrated probes in temperate loams, and the water-saving result is replicated, but the wider adoption questions remain open.

The Ashgrove Regional Health Trust replaced its outpatient appointment-booking module between March and July 2026. The legacy module had run for eleven years across four clinic sites in the county of Wendmoor, and it stored bookings in a local database that was synchronised overnight with the trust's records system. The replacement, a cloud-hosted scheduling service internally named Tessel, promised live availability, patient self-service rebooking and automated reminder messages. This post-mortem records how the migration was run, what went wrong during cutover, and what the team learned about early effects on patient attendance.

The work was carried out by a platform team of six engineers, a clinical operations lead, and two site managers who handled local communication with reception staff. The clinical operations lead owned the decision to cut over each site, and the platform team owned the data mapping and the reconciliation tooling. Most of the team's time in the first month went into a field-mapping problem. The legacy module encoded clinic sessions as free-text strings, so each session had to be parsed into a structured resource with a start time, a duration, a clinician reference and a set of permitted appointment types. About four percent of legacy session strings did not parse cleanly and had to be resolved by hand.

Cutover ran in three waves. Wave one covered the Eastfield site, which had the highest booking volume and the most experienced reception staff. Wave two covered the Marlow Road and Kestrel Court sites together. Wave three covered the orthopaedic referral clinic, which was moved last because its appointment types were the most complicated. Each wave was preceded by a dry run in which the nightly export from the legacy module was loaded into a staging copy of Tessel and compared against the live booking list. A reconciliation script produced a daily discrepancy report, and a discrepancy was counted whenever a booking existed in one system but not the other, or when the start time or clinician differed.

Wave one produced most of the useful data. Across the first nine days after the Eastfield cutover, the reconciliation report covered 2,300 bookings, and the discrepancy count fell from 61 on day one to 4 by day nine, after the parsing rules were corrected. Two results from this period are reported here as findings, but both rest on a small and short comparison and should be read as early signals rather than settled conclusions.

The first signal concerns attendance. Early results suggest that the no-show rate rose from 7.1 percent to 8.4 percent at the Eastfield site during the two weeks after cutover, compared with the same two weeks in the previous year. The difference is 1.3 percentage points, and with only 2,300 bookings the uncertainty around it is wide, roughly plus or minus 1.9 points at the usual 95 percent level. A rise of this size could reflect the new system, but it could equally reflect a different mix of appointment types in those weeks, a school holiday, or a change in how reception staff coded no-shows.

The second signal concerns duplicate bookings. In wave one, the rate of duplicate bookings, meaning two active appointments for the same patient and appointment type within a single day, fell from 1.9 per hundred bookings to 1.2 per hundred. The team believes this may be linked to the self-service rebooking flow, which shows a patient's existing appointments before they can book again. This finding is weaker than the first, because the legacy duplicate counts were produced by a nightly job whose logic was not reviewed before the migration, and the team has not confirmed that the two systems count duplicates the same way.

Waves two and three did not show the same pattern in their first week. At Marlow Road the no-show rate was flat, and at Kestrel Court the duplicate rate was briefly higher than before cutover before settling. The team therefore does not regard the Eastfield results as representative of the trust as a whole. Four sites with different patient populations, and a referral clinic with different booking rules, are too varied to be summarised by one figure from a single site.

A patient-experience survey run in June gave a conflicting picture. Of 412 responses from Marlow Road, 81 percent rated the booking experience as good or very good, which was higher than the 74 percent reported for the legacy system in 2025. The survey was voluntary, was sent only to patients who had completed a booking online, and therefore does not represent patients who booked by telephone. Its direction of effect is in tension with the Eastfield no-show signal, and the two cannot yet be reconciled.

Several assumptions shaped the analysis and have not been tested. The team assumed that the same-period comparison in the previous year was a fair baseline, although that year included a change in clinic rota patterns at two sites that was never documented in the booking data. The team also assumed that reminder messages reached the same proportion of patients in both periods, but delivery logs for the legacy system were kept for only ninety days and could not be checked for the baseline.

The post-mortem does not recommend changing reminder schedules or retiring the legacy duplicate job on the basis of these results. Before the trust acts on either signal, three conditions should be met. First, the no-show comparison should be repeated over at least one full quarter, using a matched control site that stayed on the legacy module for the same period. Second, the duplicate-counting logic in both systems should be documented and run side by side on a sample of at least 1,000 bookings. Third, the clinical operations lead should confirm that no-show coding has been applied consistently by reception staff across both periods.

Several operational lessons are less contested and may be useful to other trusts. The field-mapping work took longer than the vendor estimate, so the team recommends budgeting for manual resolution of unstructured legacy data. Dry runs proved more valuable than expected, because they exposed parsing errors that would otherwise have appeared as missed appointments. Reception staff needed a printed quick-reference card for the first fortnight after each cutover, and the team would plan for this from the start.

The migration also exposed a gap in ownership. Responsibility for the reconciliation report passed between the platform team and the site managers twice during the project, and for about three weeks in April nobody was reviewing the daily discrepancy output. The report has since been assigned to a named analyst with a weekly sign-off. Future projects should record ownership of monitoring tools at the same time as the systems they monitor.

Next steps are modest. The platform team will extend the Eastfield comparison through the end of the calendar quarter, begin the side-by-side duplicate audit, and report back to the trust's clinical governance group in January 2027. Until then, Tessel remains in use at all four sites, and the legacy module is kept in read-only mode for retrieval of historical records. The team does not expect to know whether the reminder and duplicate effects are real until the extended comparison is complete.

This safety assessment examines whether the Harbor Line fleet of autonomous forklifts can share aisles with pedestrian pickers during night operations at the Westgate distribution center, a fictional facility on the edge of the town of Calder Mills. The fleet has forty-two units built on a common chassis by the invented firm Orrin Vehicle Works. Each unit carries a spinning lidar head, two stereo cameras, and a floor-contact sensor that trips an emergency stop when a wheel leaves the marked lane. The site operations lead, Dana Pellworth, commissioned the review after night-shift supervisors asked for a clear answer before the pedestrian zones were extended. The review group had four members: two from the site engineering team, a contract safety analyst, and a logistics coordinator who handles the shift records.

The fleet was introduced two years ago, and its firmware has been updated three times since. The first update changed the lane-marking parser, the second adjusted the speed governor after a battery swap delay in the spring, and the third altered how the stop logic handles repeated detections. Maintenance is contracted to a regional workshop called Tessel Row Service, which rotates technicians on a four-week cycle. Shift records are kept in a shared spreadsheet that the logistics coordinator maintains by hand, and some night entries were typed up from paper sheets the following morning. These details matter less to the main result than the two evidence sources described below, but the team recorded them because they shape how the data can be read.

Two sources of evidence were used, and they were gathered independently. The first is a controlled trial of 1,140 scripted approach events on a closed test lane, in which a dressed mannequin stepped into the forklift path at speeds between walking pace and a brisk jog. The second is a retrospective review of 3,870 operating hours in which the fleet's own near-miss logs were coded by two reviewers working separately. The trial used the speed governor at its nominal limit, and the review covered only the day shift of the previous year, because the night logs were not complete enough to code.

In the controlled trial, the emergency stop engaged before contact in 1,118 of 1,140 approach events, a rate of about 98 percent. The 95 percent interval around that rate runs from roughly 97 to 99 percent, and the median stopping distance was 0.9 metres. The trial therefore supports the claim that the stop logic works reliably when the approach is clean, meaning when the pedestrian is standing alone in a clear lane and the sensors have an uninterrupted view.

The retrospective review told a less comfortable story. The reviewers coded 212 near-miss records, and 37 of them were classified as stops that engaged late or not at all, with the pedestrian inside 1.5 metres when the unit halted. Of those 37, 14 involved a loaded pushcart or a pallet wrapped in film, configurations that the trial did not reproduce. The two reviewers agreed on most codes, but the agreement was only moderate, and the disagreements clustered in the category for partial occlusion.

A field rate cannot be set directly beside the trial rate. The field logs record late stops but do not record how many pedestrians came near the forklifts without incident, so the team has no denominator of approach events for the day shift. Without that count, the failure rate per encounter cannot be computed from them, and any comparison with the 98 percent trial figure is a comparison of different things. The team also notes that the trial mannequin was dressed in matte grey and carried no load, which may have made its returns easier for the lidar to read than a real worker's outline against a cluttered background.

The reviewers' agreement deserves a qualification of its own. Their Cohen's kappa was 0.64, which is moderate, and the disagreements were concentrated in cases where a pedestrian was partly hidden behind a rack. Any count drawn from those cases carries the same uncertainty, so the 37 late stops should be read as a range from about 30 to about 45 rather than as a fixed number.

The two sources do not yet agree, and the review does not claim that either one is the more reliable. The trial is clean and controlled but narrow, while the field logs are messy but reflect real operation. The trial was run on a single lane at a fixed 220 lux, and no night-shift lighting was tested, even though most of the concern relates to night work. This is a limit on scope rather than a flaw in the stop logic, but it means the trial cannot be extended to the night shift on its own evidence.

The team's current reading is that the stopping system is likely to perform well in clear conditions and may underperform when loads or partial occlusion interfere with the sensors. Early results suggest that the gap is concentrated in a small set of configurations, but the sample of field events is too small to rank them with any confidence. The report therefore does not recommend sharing night aisles with pedestrian pickers at this time, and it treats the trial result as a ceiling on performance rather than an estimate of what the night floor will look like.

Before the fleet shares night-shift aisles, the team sets three conditions. First, the field logs must be re-coded against a shared denominator of approach events, drawn from the night shift and the day shift alike. Second, a second trial must include loaded pushcarts and wrapped pallets at the same lighting level used on the night floor. Third, the maintenance workshop must confirm that the spring firmware change to the stop logic was tested against those configurations. Until all three are met, the recommendation stands.

The review will go to the operations committee, which meets on the first Tuesday of each month, and a follow-up is planned for February. Dana Pellworth has asked that a plain-language summary be shared with the pickers' union representative, and the logistics coordinator will prepare the re-coded spreadsheet once the night logs are complete.

The benchmark was run by the Cell Durability Group at Halden Ridge Institute of Electrified Transport, a university-affiliated lab in the town of Pell Harrow. A regional transit authority commissioned the work because it wanted to know whether lower cost cell chemistries could safely replace the current packs in its shared e-bike fleet. The group had spent three earlier years on a bench-level study of single cells, and this project extended that work to complete packs installed in purpose-built housings. Most of the team's time in the first year went to logistics rather than measurement, since the environmental chambers needed recalibration twice and one shipment of packs was held at customs for seven weeks.

The project team had five members. The principal investigator handled the transit authority contract, a senior technician ran the chambers, and two graduate students managed cycling schedules and data cleaning. A part-time statistician reviewed the analysis plan but never visited the test site. The group met weekly over video and kept most working notes in a shared document, which the authors later summarised for this report.

Testing covered 214 packs drawn from four production lots supplied by two cell makers, Corvane Cell Works and Ostrava Field Power. Each pack ran a standard commuter profile with 80 percent depth of discharge and fast charging at 2 C for the first 60 percent of each charge. Cycling continued for up to 1,200 cycles or until capacity fell below 70 percent of rated value. One chamber held ambient temperature at 25 degrees Celsius and a second held it at 35 degrees. Capacity was checked every 50 cycles with a reference discharge at 0.5 C, which is slower than riders typically draw. Two packs were removed after a connector fault unrelated to cell behaviour, leaving 212 in the first wave. The cycle logging software was written in-house and changed version midway through, so the team compared outputs from twelve packs under both versions and found them identical to within measurement noise.

Cycling was scheduled in overnight blocks so that chamber time was shared evenly among lots. Packs were rotated between shelf positions every two weeks to limit position effects, and the rotation log shows a small number of missed swaps during the cooling failure period described below. The analysis used a mixed model with lot as a random effect, fitted to capacity retention at each 50 cycle checkpoint. Median values were taken from the fitted curves rather than raw points, which reduces the influence of single noisy readings. Packs that reached the 70 percent end point were treated as ending at that cycle, and packs still running at 1,200 cycles were treated as censored. Procurement costs were recorded separately, and the team estimated that lithium iron phosphate packs were about 18 percent cheaper per kilowatt hour at the time of purchase, though regional prices were volatile during the study.

The principal finding is that packs using lithium iron phosphate cells retained a median of 81 percent of rated capacity at 1,000 cycles under the 25 degree condition, compared with 68 percent for the nickel manganese cobalt packs. The gap held across all four production lots. A replication wave run eight months later used 96 fresh packs from a third lot and reproduced the ordering, with medians of 80 and 66 percent. Because the two waves were run by the same group with the same profile, the replication tests repeatability within this design rather than independence from it.

The 35 degree chamber ran for only 400 cycles because of a cooling failure in the second half of the year, so claims about hot conditions rest on a shorter record than the 25 degree results. The group describes the hot-chamber data as indicative only and has not published a comparison at matched cycle counts.

The confidence interval on the median difference runs roughly from 9 to 15 percentage points. That range is wide enough that a smaller effect in real riders' hands cannot be excluded. The interval was computed from pack-level data that treats packs within a lot as independent, which the authors acknowledge may understate the spread.

The results apply to packs without active thermal management and to commuter duty only. The study did not test delivery-vehicle use with heavier loads, and it did not include cold climates below freezing, where lithium iron phosphate behaviour may differ from what was observed here.

The team assumed that the reference discharge measurement reflects usable capacity in the field. Riders seldom draw at 0.5 C, and the relationship between slow-discharge capacity and range under real loads has not been checked on these packs. A short bench check on eight packs is planned but was not finished when the report was written.

A separate field log kept by the transit authority covers 60 bikes over six months. It showed no clear difference between chemistries in reported range complaints. Field riders mostly described range by feel, and the log lacks the cycle counts needed to link complaints to pack age, so the two sources cannot be reconciled directly.

Before any fleet changeover, the authority should require a thermal management review and a pilot in the intended climate. The group also recommends that any purchase contract specify capacity testing at a discharge rate closer to field use. The shared tracking spreadsheet was maintained by the two graduate students, who rotated off the project in the spring, and their handover notes are archived with the raw logs.
